Section II
APPAREL, EQUIPMENT AND MATERIALS
2-01. Apparel, General.--Torn or loose clothes should never be worn. All employees should keep their
clothing sewed, patched or in such condition that there are no flopping ends; as loose clothing is
neither safe nor comfortable. Safety shoes are recommended for all employees working on floating
plant, either in the boatyard or field. (They cost no more than ordinary shoes, and afford maximum
protection to the feet.) All safety apparel shall be adjuste

d unless authorized by the supervisors.
2-06. Goggles shall be worn while using:
(a) grinders or emory wheels,
(b) jackhammers or chippers,
(c) sand blast equipment where all operators are to wear hoods,
(d) spray guns, or brushing above one's chest,

(e) Creosote paint, caustics, etc., and will be used in any place where there is danger of a flying
particle striking an employee's eye.
(f) Sterilize goggles in alcohol before issuing to another employee.
2-07. Hood with air supply hose shall be worn:
(a) When sandblasting in confined area, where air currents cannot supply fresh air and keep
excessive dust blown away and;
(b) when painting in any confined area, where air currents cannot supply fresh air and keep excessive
fumes blown away.
2-08

confined area, where air currents cannot supply fresh air and keep excessive
fumes blown away.
2-08. Welders hoods, sleeves and gloves shall be worn whenever welding is done by the electric arc
method, when working overhead with acetylene torch, and when babbiting or soldering.
2-09. Life belts with suitable safety line shall be worn by all employees, when danger of falling is a
hazard to be encountered. A few reminders as to wearing and care are as follows:
(a) Wear life belt when oiling or re

untered. A few reminders as to wearing and care are as follows:
(a) Wear life belt when oiling or repairing masts of derricks or dipper dredges, etc.

(b) All personnel should wear life belts when working from ladders in valve pits, etc.
(c) When working on dam wickets.
(d) Life belts may be worn when working on lock gates in place of safety jackets.
(e) Belts should be inspected each day.
(f) Never punch extra holes in safety belts; get one that fits.
(g) Do not throw belts on walls, floors or ground.
(h) Belts should be cleaned and wiped dry at the end of each day's use.
(i) Leather belts should be oiled regularly with Neats foot oil or any

t the end of each day's use.
(i) Leather belts should be oiled regularly with Neats foot oil or any approved leather dressing. (Never
oil a leather object with cylinder oil).
2-10. Life jackets shall be worn by all employees performing work where there is a chance of falling,
slipping or being pushed or thrown into the water - such as
(a) on lock walls, at hand operated locks, when one man is making a lockage at night,
ng a lockage at night,

(b) when making repairs near the edge of lock wall,
(c) when working on the deck of dredges, barges or derrick boats,
(d) when drilling or sounding from the deck of boats or flats,
(e) working on lock gates,
(f) raising or lowering wickets,
(g) working on steep river banks,
(h) while in any skiff or launch.
2-11. Respirators shall be worn while
(a) using spray gun,
(b) sandblasting in the open,
(c) painting in interiors when ventilation is poor,
(d) cleaning scale from inside of boilers, and
(e)

) painting in interiors when ventilation is poor,
(d) cleaning scale from inside of boilers, and
(e) whenever and wherever there is an extraordinary amount of dust in the air, and air hoods are not
required,

2-12. Safety hats shall be worn - (a) Whenever employees are working below other employees or
plant in valve pits or lock chambers on construction or repair work, etc., where there is danger of
being struck by falling objects.
2-13. Safety foot guards, or shoes.--
(a) Foot guards are standard equipment and shall be worn by all employees working in boatyard,
machine shops, or on any repair work, or field work where heavy objects are being moved or lifted
from the floor or ground, unless the emplo

field work where heavy objects are being moved or lifted
from the floor or ground, unless the employee is wearing safety shoes. Several instances of such
work are - handling rock; placing buoys and weights; installing or replacing machinery; storing
supplies, etc.
(b) Safety shoes are not furnished by the Government, but are recommended by the Department.
They are manufactured by several leading shoe companies, and can be purchased for the same price
as a good work shoe. They are comfortable, l

shoe companies, and can be purchased for the same price
as a good work shoe. They are comfortable, long wearing shoes, and provide the nearest thing to
absolute toe and arch protection now available on the market.
2-14. Equipment General.--No employee shall use defective tools or equipment. Mushroomed heads
on chisels, etc; cracked hammer

or axe handles; loose heads, as on axes, mauls, etc; frayed rope; or weakened wire rope should be
reported to the supervisor and laid aside where they cannot be used. Never use a tool in any manner,
or in doing a task, for which it was not intended. Small tools should be held by means of tongs when
being struck by a second person. When not in use all tools should be stored in the tool locker or on
the tool board provided for them. Always examine equipment before using.
2-15. Adzes and machetes.-

the tool board provided for them. Always examine equipment before using.
2-15. Adzes and machetes.--(a) Store, and carry these tools in a sheathe, in the same manner as an
axe.
(b) Never use an adze on a loose board; work in a clear space; concentrate on your work; and never
chop towards your foot.
(c) Never use a machete in a cramped position; chop away from the body; watch for approaching
employees. Watch for overhead vines and limbs. Do not use a machete in any place where the
footing is not

yees. Watch for overhead vines and limbs. Do not use a machete in any place where the
footing is not secure. Keep right leg forward if using machete in right hand and left leg forward if using
in left hand.
2-16. Axes.--(a) 1. General.--When not in use they shall be stored in racks or fastened to the wall in
such manner that they cannot shake loose and fall.

2. When being carried in a vehicle the blade should be encased, so that no part of the sharpened
edge is exposed. Only single edge axes are recommended for use; and if being carried on the job
should be shouldered with the blunt end toward the neck.
3. Hazards to be avoided when chopping are overhanging limbs and vines; chopping towards feet, or
other parts of the body; approach of other employees; flying chips; loose heads; dull blades; and
above all uncertain footing should be avoided.
(b) Han

; flying chips; loose heads; dull blades; and
above all uncertain footing should be avoided.
(b) Hand axes.--1. Heads should be single blade, carried in a sheathe provided with belt loop and
fastener to prevent the axe from falling out. The cutting edge should be kept sharp and clean at all
times. It should be solidly wedged on the handle.
2. Handles shall be straight, sound, clear and free from defects.
3. Use.--Never throw an axe. Never chop toward the body. Do not use an axe in a confined or

efects.
3. Use.--Never throw an axe. Never chop toward the body. Do not use an axe in a confined or
crowded area. Be alert for approaching employees. If it becomes necessary to clear out overhead
branches out of reach from the ground, the axe should be carried up the tree in the belt sheathe, on
the belt; or preferably, raised by means of a handy line.

(c) Pole axes.--1. Heads should be single bit and solidly wedged to the handle. The cutting edge
should be kept sharp and clean at all times.
2. Handles shall be straight, sound, clear and free from defects.
3. Use.--A pole axe should not be used as a sledge hammer, as it will spread the eye, causing the
handle to become loose and dangerous. Before using a pole axe be certain that there is no brush to
obstruct a clear swing. Look the tree over for any dead limbs that may become disengaged during

h to
obstruct a clear swing. Look the tree over for any dead limbs that may become disengaged during the
chopping or felling of the tree. Make a deep "V" grooved notch on the side that the tree is to fall. This
will prevent kick backs. Axe should be carried on shoulder with the cutting edge away from neck.
(d) Double-Bit axes.--1. Heads are double-bladed and should be solidly wedged to the handle. The
cutting edges should be kept sharp and clean. Excessive grinding on one edge will cause the axe

The
cutting edges should be kept sharp and clean. Excessive grinding on one edge will cause the axe to
become unbalanced and dangerous.
2. Handles shall be straight, sound, clear, and free from defects.
3. Use.--A double-bit axe should never be used on the side, as a hammer, to drive wedges or stakes.
Double-bit axes are

not recommended, but when necessary shall be used only by experienced axemen. Never work in
confined areas. Clear away all brush, low limbs and obstructing vines.
2-17. Chains.--(a) Examination.--1. Inspect every link in a chain whenever the chain has not been
used for a considerable length of time, or, whenever the chain is to be used for heavy lifting that will
strain the capacity of the chain.
2. Check the hook and ring for weakness, spread or crimp.
(b) Use.--1. Do not overload a chain.
2. N

2. Check the hook and ring for weakness, spread or crimp.
(b) Use.--1. Do not overload a chain.
2. Never put hands between a chain and the object it is wrapped around.
3. Never repair chain with wire. (Use a cold shut or similar repair link).
4. Wrap chain around object, and fasten. Do not lift object with hook, unless special fastenings are
used. Tie hook securely so that it will not come loose, or slip.
2-18. Chisels.--(a) Wood chisels should never be used except for the purpose they are inten

or slip.
2-18. Chisels.--(a) Wood chisels should never be used except for the purpose they are intended and
should never be directed towards the body. Use wooden mallets; see

that handle and point are solid and in good repair; keep the cutting edge sharp and true.
(b) Cold chisels.--Cold chisels should be checked for defects before use. Chisels with mushroomed
heads, broken points and cracked shanks should be removed from service until properly repaired.
Never direct the point toward the body. Use proper hammer; keep the cutting edge sharp.
2-19. Drills.--Drills for drilling into masonry or rock should never be used for crow bars. Shanks must
be straight; cutting edg

illing into masonry or rock should never be used for crow bars. Shanks must
be straight; cutting edges sharp; and heads flat without mushrooms.
2-20. Files.--Files shall be provided with handles. Whenever the material being filed is fastened in a
machine or being turned by mechanical means, the operator should roll up his sleeves, and remove
tie if one is being worn.
2-21. Fire Extinguishers.--(a) General.--Extinguishers shall be located by the Safety Section in readily
accessible places, and sh

General.--Extinguishers shall be located by the Safety Section in readily
accessible places, and shall be examined every month. The initials of the examiner shall be placed
on the card with the date of each examination.
(b) Carbon Tetrachloride extinguishers shall be placed on all floating plant and houses, storehouses
and garages, trucks and passenger cars. Keep recharges on hand for

each type. It is to be used on indoor fires in wood textiles, paper, rubbish, etc. It is not so effective
outdoors where wind strikes the fire. It is fairly effective on all types of fire except electrical.
(c) CO2 extinguishers shall be placed in all floating plant, where highly inflammable materials are
stored, ie, gasoline, paint, etc. They shall be tested by weighing every six months and if more than
one pound under-weight shall be recharged immediately. This is the best type for fires invol

re than
one pound under-weight shall be recharged immediately. This is the best type for fires involving oil,
grease, paint, lacquer, etc., where the smothering action is effective.
(d) Soda-acid extinguishers which contain water as an extinguishing agent, and soda and sulphuric
acid as the pressure agent to expel the water through the hose, WILL FREEZE and must be kept in
protected places where the temperature will not be below 32 Fahrenheit. These extinguishers are for
use in fighting fires in

he temperature will not be below 32 Fahrenheit. These extinguishers are for
use in fighting fires in free burning material such as wood, paper, rubbish, etc. Under no
circumstances should they be used for electrical fires because the water conducts the current back to
the body of the operator. A sign will be placed on the soda acid extinguisher to this effect. These
extinguishers shall be refilled once each year and immediately after being discharged in case of
emergency. To keep the nozzle clea

once each year and immediately after being discharged in case of
emergency. To keep the nozzle clear,

wire shall be run through nozzle at least once each month.
2-22. Hammers and mauls.--(a) Keep the heads dressed, never use a mushroomed, battered, or
chipped tool.
(b) Use bronze, babbitt or wooden mallet for striking metal parts such as tapping keys out of drill
chucks, when sustained hammering is unnecessary.
(c) Check handles and fastenings of heads before using.
(d) Keep eyes on work.
2-23. Jacks.--(a) Overload should never be placed on a jack.
(b) Footing.--Always place a jack on a solid, l

cks.--(a) Overload should never be placed on a jack.
(b) Footing.--Always place a jack on a solid, level footing.
(c) Blocking.--Keep blocking on each side of load center to within 1" of jack height.
(d) Don't get under loads supported only by a jack, without blocking.
2-24. Ladders.--(a) General.--Ladders should never be painted. Use linseed oil or clear varnish.
(b) Climbing ladders.--1. Examine for defects before using.
for defects before using.

2. Use ladder with safety feet, and if floor is hard or slippery tie ladder at base or have someone hold
it.
3. Place base of ladder about 1/4 of length from wall.
4. Face ladder and hold on to side rails with both hands, whether ascending or descending.
5. Clean soles of shoes before climbing.
6. Never use a ladder in front of a doorway, unless door is locked or guarded.
7. If rungs are slippery, clean off before raising the ladder.
8. Carry all tools in suitable pockets, or hoist them in a sac

clean off before raising the ladder.
8. Carry all tools in suitable pockets, or hoist them in a sack with rope.
(c) Step ladders.--1. Be certain that legs are fully extended.
2. Lock the spreader.
3. If footing is slippery block the feet.
4. Avoid standing on top, use long enough ladder to stand at least 2 steps from

top.
5. Never lay tools on ladder. A suitable box should be provided to hold tools.
(d) Extension ladders.--1. Raising an extension ladder is a two man job.
2. Raise ladder before extending it.
3. Use rope or pole to extend ladder.
4. When lowering, reverse the process.
(e) Use of ladders.--1. Never use a ladder for a scaffold plank or walkway.
2. Carry ladder with safety feet to the rear.
3. When carrying a ladder alone, stand at the balance point of the weight, and elevate the front to a
heigh

carrying a ladder alone, stand at the balance point of the weight, and elevate the front to a
height above a person's head.
4. If ceilings are low carry ladder at side.
5. When two persons are carrying a ladder, they should stand as near the ends as possible.

6. Be careful not to strike anyone with the ladder.
7. Never lean far out from any ladder.
8. Use safety line when work requires it.
9. Do not work from a ladder in a high wind.
10. If working over a walkway, where people might be hit by falling objects, rope off the space around
and under the ladder.
2-25. Pneumatic tools.--Pneumatic tools shall never be pointed at a person.
(a) Safety clips shall be fastened before using.
(b) Protect the ear drums, before commencing work, in a confined area by

l be fastened before using.
(b) Protect the ear drums, before commencing work, in a confined area by placing cotton in ears.
(c) Air hose shall not be pointed towards the body.
(d) Do not use air hose for cleaning structures, unless all persons in vicinity have on goggles.

In emergencies, control of the flow, of water in a distribution system 
is secondary only to the need for an adequate supply of water. Proper 
operation of the system under these conditions requires the availability 
of complete and accurate maps and records of all mains, valves, connec-
tions, and other appurtenances in the system. These records are also 
necessary for promptly shutting off fractured mains and for making 
emergency repairs and re

necessary for promptly shutting off fractured mains and for making

system in an emergency is a comprehensive or arterial map showing 
all fire hydrants and mains to scale. Such a map will indicate how 
the system may best be operated to supply a maximum amount of water 
to critical areas, the capacity of the system for supplying water to 
any area threatened by conflagration, and the are

the capacity of the system for supplying water to 
any area threatened by conflagration, and the areas in which low 
pressures are likely to develop when the system is subjected to excessive 
demands. Comprehensive maps are also useful for spotting main 
breaks, recording progress of repair operations, and noting locations 
of conflagrations and areas deprived of service.
Often, distribution system records are considered secondary to 
engineering work, with the result that changes and repairs ar

misleading records. For example, valves which the records show to

inspections of the valves and by keeping records accurate and up

REPAIR OF WATER MAINS
General
Experience in this war has demonstrated the vulnerability of water 
distribution systems to aerial attack. Any high-explosive bomb 
dropped in a street will generally fracture all nearby water pipes and 
sewers. Pipes located 70 to 100 feet from the bomb burst are fre-
quently fractured. In clay soil or rock, the distance may be greater, 
depending on the size of bomb and the type of backfill around the pipe.

In event of aerial attack or other disaster affecting a distribution 
system, prompt repair of fractured water mains is vital. The supply 
of water for fire fighting may have been interrupted by the break, 
and the community may have been deprived of water for domestic, 
sanitary, and industrial purposes.
If repairs are to be made promptly, it is necessary that waterworks 
engineers have a thorough knowledge of methods for making emer-

adequate supply of materials and equipment available.

When a water system becomes contaminated, the mains and other

be safely returned to service. The importance of this during disaster,

Principles of Disinfection
Proper disinfection requires that the agent used, generally chlorine, 
be uniformly dispersed throughout the system and that it reach all 
surfaces to be treated in sufficient concentration and for a period long 
enough to destroy all pathogenic bacteria. The contact period for 
proper disinfection depends upon the dosage of the d

proper disinfection depends upon the dosage of the disinfecting agent 
and the distribution of polluted material that must be penetrated. 
For thoroughly flushed surfaces a contact period of 4 to 24 hours is 
usually recommended for a dosage of 50 parts per million of chlorine. 
If service must be resumed quickly, the contact period may be reduced 
to 1 hour by increasing the chlorine dosage to 100 or 200 parts per 
million.

It is sometimes believed that fire pumpers can increase the supply 
of water by simply furnishing increased pressure for the fire stream. 
Actual tests or simple calculations will disprove this belief. Fire 
pumpers can increase the total supply only by the amount that will 
result from decreasing the residual pressure in the main at the 
hydrant. The total quantity of water that can be delivered to a fire

investigation of a distribution system, they do not disclose how the 
entire system will perform when subjected to excessive fire demands 
or how a system may be most expeditiously operated in time of emer-
gency. This information can be obtained from mathematical an-
alyses or model studies for various operating conditions. The

At first glance, the analysed set forth in this section may appear 
somewhat complicated, but closer scrutiny will show that they require 
only an understanding of the basic principles of hydraulic pipe flow, 
simple arithmetic, and the use of a pipe-flow nomograph, diagram, or 
slide rule.

or sources, of supply to any point of convergent or divergent flow are 
balanced, regardless of the path of travel. This balance of flow is 
accomplished by assuming a flow distribution for a given set of 
operating conditions and making successive approximations by apply-

head losses within each of the various circuits are equalized. Flow in 
the pipe networks must also be such that the total flow reaching any 
junction of two or more pipes will equal the flow leaving it. In case 
there is excessive leakage or closed valves in the system, allowance must

Effects of bombs on buildings.
The effect of bombing on buildings depends on the type and size 
of bomb, length of time-delay of fuse, height of release, angle of 
impact, and on the type and construction of the building. Apart from 
the damage resulting from impact and fire, the effects of high-explo-
sive bombs are due to fragments, blast, and shock. Fragments of 
bombs ordinarily do not affect the structural stability of building

blast, and shock. Fragments of 
bombs ordinarily do not affect the structural stability of buildings, 
but if a bomb explodes close to concrete beams or columns, the frag-
ments may cause severe damage. Fragments may pierce ordinary 
walls, windows, and partitions and cause extensive damage to ma-
chinery and equipment within the plant. Blast and shock are espe-
cially damaging to wall-bearing brick or masonry structures; steel 
framed and reinforced concrete buildings are less affected by near

ick or masonry structures; steel 
framed and reinforced concrete buildings are less affected by nearby 
blasts. No building will withstand a direct hit by a heavy bomb, 
unless especially designed for this purpose, but certain precautions 
can be taken to minimize the effects of nearby blasts and incendiary 
bombs.

As absolute protection against bombing is not practical except in 
special cases, the main objective in protective construction for water 
plants sh

of structures as a result of explosions in the vicinity. The provision of 
protective construction will be governed by the probabili

losions in the vicinity. The provision of

5. REPORTING AND DOCUMENTATION
All inspection findings must be recorded in the Inspection Report Form (IRF-2024). The report must
include: date and time of inspection, equipment ID and location, inspector name and certification
number, detailed findings with severity classification (Critical, Major, Minor), recommended corrective
actions, and a follow-up schedule.
6. SAFETY REQUIREMENTS
Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) procedures must be followed before inspecting any energized equipment.
